key_insight: Introducing an anchoring mechanism during training aligns independently trained predictors so their expected squared prediction difference (model disagreement) can be driven to (or toward) zero by tuning natural training parameters such as anchor strength or sample size. This gives a simple, analyzable handle for controlling disagreement in real‑valued prediction tasks.
problem_solved: How to measure and control model disagreement — the expected squared difference between predictions of models trained independently — so independently trained models produce consistent outputs without coordinating training processes.
method: Define model disagreement as the expected squared difference between two predictors trained on independent samples and derive conditions under which disagreement can be reduced.

Introduce an anchoring term or anchor-based training protocol that biases each model toward a common reference (anchor) during learning, producing bounds that show disagreement decreases with anchor strength and/or sample size.
Theoretical analysis (and supporting experiments) that quantify the tradeoffs between anchor strength, sample complexity, and predictive accuracy.
impact: Provides a practical, theoretically grounded tool for practitioners who need reproducible, consistent predictions across independently trained models — useful for deployment stability, auditing, and reducing variance-driven failures. Anchoring can be adopted with minimal changes to standard training pipelines.
visual_elements: Schematic: two independent training pipelines both receiving data and an anchor signal, converging to similar predictors
Chart: disagreement (expected squared difference) vs. anchor strength and vs. sample size showing monotonic decrease
Equation inset: clear statement of the disagreement metric (E[(f1(x) - f2(x))^2]) and the anchoring loss term
Table/plot: tradeoff between accuracy and disagreement for several anchor strengths (small accuracy cost for large agreement gain)
paper_authors: Eric Eaton, Surbhi Goel, Marcel Hussing, Michael Kearns, Aaron Roth
